claims.text: The as-processed refractory high-entropy alloy has significant atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Rapid processing produces a controlled phase balance in the as-processed alloy.
A targeted annealing treatment can selectively reduce residual strains and chemical heterogeneities in the alloy.
The targeted annealing treatment can reduce lattice distortion without changing the overall phase composition.
Reducing lattice distortion produces fewer local stress concentrations.
Fewer local stress concentrations reduce resistance to dislocation motion.
Reduced resistance to dislocation motion lowers yield strength.
Reducing lattice distortion decreases the sensitivity of elastic modulus to temperature.
The annealed alloy will have lower room-temperature yield strength than the as-processed baseline.
The annealed alloy will have lower elevated-temperature yield strength than the as-processed baseline.
The annealed alloy will show a less pronounced decrease in elastic modulus with increasing temperature than the as-processed baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to service temperatures of approximately 900 degrees Celsius.
The proposed interpretation is conditional on annealing not changing the phase balance.
Annealing may subtly modify precipitate distributions and thereby affect the observed response.

contradictions.description: The boundary conditions make unchanged phase balance a prerequisite for testing the mechanism, but the falsification rule treats an annealing-induced phase change as falsification. A phase change would instead violate the controlled-comparison condition and confound the test.
